text.p: Here are the highlights of stories in the Danish press on Thursday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

--Denmark is considering imposing a quota on the number of Norwegian students it is prepared to accept, saying that its medical schools are becoming saturated with Norwegians. Agreement from the other member countries of the Nordic Union, which gives free right of movement and residence among the states, would be necessary first.
--The fraud squad is launching an offensive against fraudulent investment salesmen, saying that telephone sales of dubious speculative offers has mushroomed of late.
--The housing ministry is to blacklist sloppy builders in an attempt to improve construction standards.

--Environment Minister Svend Auken is to ask East Asiatic Company (EAC) to give a full account of the safety measures it imposes on Thai users of Paraquat weedkiller, which the firm produces in a joint venture there. The product is banned in Denmark.
--The perception that Danish business has an unusually high tax burden is a myth, needlessly scaring off foreign investors, according to a survey by accountants KPMG C. Jespersen.

At 34 percent Danish corporation tax is lower than Germany's and around the same as Britain and the Netherlands. Sweden's 28 percent is lower but costs are swelled by higher insurance and pension payments, the survey says.
--Denmark is heading for a housing shortage, compounded by the abolition of mortgage interest tax relief, with some 230,000 fewer homes available in 10 years time, a new forecast shows.
